title: Upper limb: which nerve does each injury threaten?
text:
Anterior shoulder dislocation and surgical neck fracture: axillary nerve (numb 'regimental badge' patch, weak deltoid); check before and after reduction. Midshaft or spiral distal-third humeral fracture (Holstein-Lewis): radial nerve in the spiral groove (wrist drop, triceps spared).
Supracondylar fracture in children, extension type: posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment tents the brachial artery and median nerve, and the anterior interosseous nerve is the nerve most often injured (weak 'OK' sign, no sensory loss); posteromedial displacement stretches the radial nerve; flexion-type fractures and pin fixation from the medial side threaten the ulnar nerve. Medial epicondyle fracture: ulnar nerve. Monteggia fracture-dislocation: posterior interosseous nerve (finger drop without wrist drop).
Lunate or perilunate dislocation and distal radius fracture: median nerve (acute carpal tunnel syndrome needs urgent decompression). Hook of hamate fracture: deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Clavicle fracture rarely injures the subclavian vessels or brachial plexus beneath it.

title: Lower limb: which nerve or vessel does each injury threaten?
text:
Posterior hip dislocation (knee striking the dashboard) and posterior wall acetabular fractures: sciatic nerve in about 10%, mostly its common fibular division (foot drop). Anterior hip dislocation: femoral nerve and vessels. Vertical shear pelvic and sacral fractures through the foramina: lumbosacral roots, especially L5 as it crosses the sacral ala; anterior ring fractures may injure the obturator nerve, and the superior gluteal artery can bleed from the greater sciatic notch.
Knee dislocation: the popliteal artery, tethered at the adductor hiatus and soleal arch, is injured in up to a third, so ankle-brachial index or CT angiography is mandatory even with pulses; the common fibular nerve is injured especially with posterolateral corner disruption. Fibular neck fracture or a tight plaster: common fibular nerve. Proximal tibial fracture: the anterior tibial artery as it passes through the interosseous membrane, and compartment syndrome. Ankle fracture-dislocation and calcaneal fractures: tibial nerve and posterior tibial artery in the tarsal tunnel.

title: Preganglionic root avulsion versus postganglionic plexus injury
text:
The dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of sensory neurones. If the root is torn out of the cord (preganglionic avulsion, as in high-energy motorcycle traction injuries), the sensory axon distal to the ganglion stays attached to its cell body and does not degenerate: sensory nerve action potentials in the anaesthetic limb are PRESERVED, a paradox that proves avulsion. A postganglionic lesion separates the axon from the ganglion, so SNAPs are lost.
Clinical clues to avulsion: Horner syndrome (T1), winging of the scapula from long thoracic nerve paralysis and rhomboid weakness from dorsal scapular nerve paralysis (both arise directly from the roots), paralysis of the hemidiaphragm (phrenic), neuropathic pain and pseudomeningoceles on MRI myelography. Avulsed roots cannot be repaired directly, so function is restored by nerve transfers (for example an ulnar nerve fascicle to the biceps branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, or the spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve); postganglionic ruptures can be grafted.

targets: Branches of posterior cord of brachial plexus
title: Posterior cord lesions and crutch palsy
text:
The posterior cord gives the upper and lower subscapular nerves (subscapularis and teres major), the thoracodorsal nerve (latissimus dorsi) and ends as the axillary and radial nerves. It lies behind the second part of the axillary artery beneath pectoralis minor.
Pressure in the axilla from badly fitted crutches, a drunken sleep with an arm over a chair back or a malpositioned arm during anaesthesia injures the posterior cord or radial nerve high in the axilla: wrist and finger drop, weak elbow extension (triceps involved, unlike a spiral groove lesion) and, with posterior cord lesions, deltoid and latissimus weakness with sensory loss over the regimental badge area and back of the arm, forearm and hand. Crutches should be adjusted to bear weight through the hands with a gap below the axilla. Anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humeral fractures can also stretch the cord.

title: Superficial radial nerve: Wartenberg syndrome and cannulation injury
text:
The superficial branch of the radial nerve emerges from under brachioradialis about 8 cm above the radial styloid and runs subcutaneously over the anatomical snuffbox to supply the skin of the dorsoradial hand, the dorsum of the thumb and the lateral fingers to the middle phalanx. Being purely sensory and superficial, it is compressed by tight watch straps, plaster casts and handcuffs (cheiralgia paraesthetica or Wartenberg syndrome): burning and numbness over the back of the thumb and first web space with a positive Tinel sign, and no weakness.
It runs alongside the cephalic vein at the wrist ('intern's vein'), so cannulation there can cause painful neuromas, and it is at risk in surgery for de Quervain tenosynovitis and when placing distal radius K-wires. Injury can trigger complex regional pain syndrome.

title: Venepuncture nerve injuries in the cubital fossa
text:
The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve (the terminal sensory branch of the musculocutaneous nerve) emerges lateral to the biceps tendon deep to the cephalic vein; the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve accompanies the basilic vein on the medial side. Both run intimately with the superficial veins and can be speared during venepuncture or cannulation, causing sudden electric-shock pain and persistent paraesthesia along the lateral or medial forearm.
Deep, blind medial punctures also risk the median nerve and brachial artery, which lie medial to the biceps tendon under the bicipital aponeurosis, so the median cubital vein near the midline is the safest site. The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve can also be compressed by the biceps tendon and aponeurosis with forceful elbow extension and pronation, and is used as a sensory nerve graft.

title: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
text:
The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve about 5 cm above the wrist crease and passes SUPERFICIAL to the flexor retinaculum to supply the skin of the thenar eminence and central palm. Carpal tunnel syndrome therefore spares sensation over the thenar eminence while affecting the lateral three and a half digits; numbness of the thenar skin points to a more proximal median nerve lesion (pronator syndrome, forearm or arm).
The branch runs between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus, so a carpal tunnel release incision is placed in line with the radial border of the ring finger, ulnar to it, to avoid a painful neuroma. It is also at risk when harvesting flexor carpi radialis or palmaris longus tendons and in volar approaches to the distal radius.

title: Localising ulnar nerve lesions at the wrist
text:
The dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve leaves 5 to 8 cm above the wrist and supplies the dorsal ulnar hand and fingers. Loss of this dorsal sensation places a lesion at or above the forearm (commonly the cubital tunnel), whereas a lesion in Guyon's canal spares it.
Guyon's canal, between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate under the volar carpal ligament, has three zones. Zone 1 (proximal to the bifurcation): mixed motor and sensory loss. Zone 2 (deep motor branch): weakness and wasting of the interossei, adductor pollicis and ulnar lumbricals with normal sensation, typically from a ganglion, cycling ('handlebar palsy'), or a hook of hamate fracture; if the lesion is distal to the hypothenar branches, abductor digiti minimi is spared. Zone 3 (superficial branch): sensory loss over the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger only. Froment sign (thumb IP flexion when gripping paper, substituting flexor pollicis longus for adductor pollicis) tests the deep branch.

targets: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
title: Morton neuroma
text:
Perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve where it passes beneath the deep transverse metatarsal ligament, most often in the third intermetatarsal space, where the nerve is thickened by a communicating branch between the medial and lateral plantar nerves and relatively tethered. It is commonest in women wearing tight, high-heeled shoes that squeeze the metatarsal heads and hyperextend the toes.
Patients describe burning forefoot pain radiating into the third and fourth toes, 'like walking on a pebble', relieved by removing the shoe. Squeezing the metatarsal heads together while pressing the web space produces a painful click (Mulder sign). Ultrasound confirms it. Treatment is wide shoes and a metatarsal pad, steroid injection, or excision through a dorsal incision, which leaves numbness of the adjacent toe surfaces.

title: Baxter nerve entrapment and jogger's foot
text:
The tibial nerve divides in the tarsal tunnel into medial and lateral plantar nerves, which pass deep to abductor hallucis into the sole. The first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (inferior calcaneal or Baxter nerve) runs laterally between the deep fascia of abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae to supply abductor digiti minimi. Its entrapment causes chronic medial heel pain that is often mislabelled plantar fasciitis; clues are burning pain, tenderness over the abductor hallucis rather than the fascia origin, and fatty atrophy of abductor digiti minimi on MRI.
Jogger's foot is compression of the medial plantar nerve at the knot of Henry, where flexor digitorum longus crosses flexor hallucis longus, often provoked by an arch support orthotic: burning medial arch pain radiating to the medial toes during running.

title: Anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome
text:
The deep fibular nerve passes beneath the inferior extensor retinaculum on the front of the ankle, beside the dorsalis pedis artery between the tendons of extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus. It supplies extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis and ends as the dorsal digital nerves to the adjacent sides of the first and second toes.
Compression by tight shoe laces or ski boots, dorsal talonavicular osteophytes or ganglia causes pain on the dorsum of the foot and numbness confined to the first web space, sometimes with wasting of extensor digitorum brevis (a hollow over the lateral dorsum). Numbness of the first web space is also the earliest sign of anterior compartment syndrome, because the nerve runs through that compartment.

title: Superficial fibular nerve entrapment and portal injury
text:
The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment, then pierces the crural fascia about 10 to 12 cm above the lateral malleolus to supply the skin of the lower lateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot (sparing the first web space and lateral border).
It can be trapped where it pierces the fascia, especially after recurrent inversion sprains or with a fascial hernia, causing pain and numbness over the dorsum of the foot worse with activity. Lesions at this level cause no weakness; a lesion higher up adds weak eversion. The nerve can often be seen or felt under the skin with the foot plantarflexed and inverted, which is done before placing the anterolateral ankle arthroscopy portal, its commonest iatrogenic injury. Fasciotomy of the lateral compartment and lateral ankle surgery are other risks.

title: Saphenous nerve injury and the adductor canal block
text:
The saphenous nerve, the longest sensory branch of the femoral nerve, runs through the adductor canal with the femoral vessels, emerges between sartorius and gracilis at the knee and descends with the great saphenous vein to the medial foot. Its infrapatellar branch crosses in front of the knee to the skin below the patella.
Injuries: stripping or harvest of the great saphenous vein below the knee (numbness of the medial leg, so stripping is usually limited to the thigh), medial arthroscopy portals, hamstring graft harvest and total knee replacement incisions (a numb patch lateral to the scar from infrapatellar branch division, occasionally a painful neuroma).
The adductor canal block anaesthetises the saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis in mid-thigh for knee surgery, giving analgesia with much less quadriceps weakness (and fewer falls) than a femoral nerve block.

title: Sural nerve: biopsy, graft and injury
text:
The sural nerve, formed from medial sural (tibial) and communicating fibular branches, runs with the small saphenous vein lateral to the calcaneal tendon and behind the lateral malleolus to supply the lateral border of the foot. Because it is purely sensory, accessible and leaves only a small area of numbness, it is the standard nerve for biopsy (vasculitic neuropathy, amyloidosis, CIDP, leprosy) and the commonest donor nerve for autografts. Sural nerve conduction is part of every neuropathy study; the classic length-dependent 'glove and stocking' neuropathy affects it early.
It is at risk in small saphenous vein surgery, percutaneous Achilles tendon repair, lateral approaches to the calcaneus and fifth metatarsal fixation, producing numbness or a painful neuroma on the lateral foot.

title: Groin nerves: hernia repair pain and the cremasteric reflex
text:
The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) run between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis and pierce internal oblique near the anterior superior iliac spine. The ilioinguinal nerve then travels through the inguinal canal on the spermatic cord (or round ligament) to supply the upper medial thigh and the root of the penis and anterior scrotum or mons and labium majus. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2) enters the deep ring and supplies cremaster and the scrotal skin.
They are injured or trapped by sutures and mesh in inguinal hernia repair (chronic post-herniorrhaphy groin pain in up to 10%), by Pfannenstiel and appendicectomy incisions and by laparoscopic tacks, causing burning pain radiating to the genitalia and thigh. Ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric blocks medial to the ASIS are used for paediatric hernia surgery.
The cremasteric reflex (stroking the medial thigh elevates the testis, L1-L2) is typically absent in testicular torsion.

title: Dorsal scapular nerve entrapment
text:
The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root, pierces scalenus medius and runs down beneath levator scapulae and the rhomboids along the medial border of the scapula. Entrapment in a hypertrophied scalenus medius (weightlifters, overhead workers) or injury during interscalene block causes aching medial scapular and interscapular pain, weakness of the rhomboids and levator scapulae and subtle lateral winging of the medial border when the arm is lowered from full elevation.
Because the nerve comes straight off the root, rhomboid weakness in a brachial plexus injury indicates a very proximal (C5 root) lesion. It must be distinguished from long thoracic nerve palsy (medial winging on pushing against a wall) and trapezius palsy from accessory nerve injury (lateral winging with shoulder drooping).

title: Interscalene, supraclavicular and axillary brachial plexus blocks
text:
The roots and trunks of the brachial plexus emerge between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius. An interscalene block at the level of C6 anaesthetises C5-C7 and is ideal for shoulder surgery, but often spares C8-T1 (ulnar territory), so it is poor for hand surgery. The phrenic nerve lies on the front of scalenus anterior, so ipsilateral hemidiaphragmatic paralysis is almost universal; the block is avoided in severe lung disease or a contralateral phrenic palsy. Other effects: Horner syndrome, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal block, and rare vertebral artery, epidural or intrathecal injection.
The supraclavicular block targets the compact trunks and divisions above the first rib (the 'spinal of the arm'), with pneumothorax as the main risk. The axillary block surrounds the axillary artery for forearm and hand surgery, but the musculocutaneous nerve leaves the sheath high, inside coracobrachialis, and must be blocked separately.

title: Femoral nerve and fascia iliaca blocks for hip fracture
text:
In the femoral triangle the structures run lateral to medial as nerve, artery, vein, empty space and lymphatics (NAVEL). The femoral nerve lies LATERAL to the femoral sheath, deep to the fascia iliaca on the iliopsoas, so local anaesthetic must be placed beneath the fascia iliaca, not just beside the artery.
The fascia iliaca compartment block, injected beneath the fascia lateral to the nerve (landmark: the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the inguinal ligament, or by ultrasound), spreads to the femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves and gives effective, opioid-sparing analgesia for hip fractures in the emergency department, reducing delirium in the elderly. Blocks near the femoral nerve weaken the quadriceps, so patients must be protected from falls. The femoral artery pulse, at the midinguinal point, guides the approach.

title: Ankle block: five nerves
text:
The foot is supplied by five nerves, all accessible at the ankle, which allows forefoot surgery under local anaesthesia. Two are deep: the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus beside the posterior tibial artery (sole of the foot), and the deep fibular nerve on the front of the ankle beside the dorsalis pedis artery between the extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus tendons (first web space). Three are superficial and blocked by a subcutaneous ring: the superficial fibular nerve across the front of the ankle (most of the dorsum), the sural nerve between the lateral malleolus and the calcaneal tendon (lateral border), and the saphenous nerve in front of the medial malleolus with the great saphenous vein (medial ankle and foot).
Knowing these territories also localises sensory loss in neuropathy and after trauma.

targets: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
title: Digital nerve injury and ring block
text:
Each finger has two palmar digital nerves running along the palmar-lateral and palmar-medial sides, just palmar to (in front of) the digital arteries, plus small dorsal branches. Palmar lacerations often divide them: always test sensation, ideally two-point discrimination (normal under 6 mm at the fingertip), BEFORE giving local anaesthetic, and remember that sweating ceases in a denervated fingertip. Digital nerves are repaired under magnification because an unrepaired nerve leaves a numb, vulnerable finger and a painful neuroma.
A digital (ring) block injects anaesthetic at the base of the finger on both sides, or as a single palmar subcutaneous injection. Adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic is now considered safe in healthy fingers (the old warning was based on procaine-era cases), but it is avoided with vascular disease or Raynaud phenomenon.

title: Inferior alveolar block, lingual nerve injury and numb chin
text:
The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen on the medial side of the ramus, guarded by the lingula, supplies all lower teeth on that side and emerges from the mental foramen below the second premolar as the mental nerve to the lower lip and chin. The lingual nerve lies just anterior and medial in the pterygomandibular space. An inferior alveolar block, injected medial to the ramus above the foramen, numbs the teeth, lip and chin and usually the tongue as well. Needling too far posteriorly deposits anaesthetic in the parotid gland, causing a transient facial nerve palsy; medial pterygoid injury causes trismus.
The lingual nerve lies against the lingual cortex beside the lower third molar, so wisdom tooth extraction can injure it (numbness and loss of taste on the anterior tongue from the chorda tympani fibres it carries); the inferior alveolar nerve can be damaged by roots that lie near the canal.
'Numb chin syndrome', unexplained mental nerve numbness, may be the first sign of metastatic cancer (breast, lymphoma, prostate) in the mandible or skull base.

title: Transversus abdominis plane and rectus sheath blocks
text:
The anterior rami of T7 to L1 (the thoracoabdominal, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves) run forward in the neurovascular plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis before entering the rectus sheath. Local anaesthetic spread in this plane (the transversus abdominis plane, TAP) under ultrasound, or through the lumbar triangle of Petit in the original landmark technique, numbs the skin, muscles and parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall.
TAP blocks give analgesia after caesarean section, hernia repair and laparoscopic surgery; lateral injections cover roughly T10-L1 and subcostal injections the upper abdomen. They do NOT block visceral pain. A rectus sheath block, between the rectus and its posterior sheath, covers midline incisions. The same plane explains why these nerves can be damaged by lateral port sites and oblique incisions, causing a denervated bulge.
